analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers to tell customers what they actually pay for medical services.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a single cosponsor or any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The True Price Act would have required health insurers and employer health plans to tell enrollees the negotiated rate the plan pays for each covered health service, plus any copay or coinsurance the enrollee owes. Insurers would have had to post this price information on their websites and provide a paper copy on request, starting January 1, 2020. It never advanced past its first step in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: People with health insurance, who today often cannot find out what their insurer actually pays a doctor or hospital, or what their share will be, until a bill arrives. Seeing negotiated rates and cost-sharing in advance would let patients compare prices and avoid surprise charges.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured patients facing opaque medical bills

how_it_helps.text: Requires insurers and employer plans to disclose to enrollees the negotiated rate paid for each covered health care service, including what the plan pays and what the enrollee owes in cost-sharing.
Requires that price information be posted on the insurer's website, with a hard copy available on request, so patients can see prices before getting care rather than after the bill arrives.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer health plans, which would have to compile, publish, and keep current the negotiated rates for every service they cover, and would lose some ability to keep those rates confidential. Hospitals and providers whose negotiated prices are well below list prices would have that pricing exposed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: A single posted rate does not equal a clear price: an enrollee's actual bill still depends on which doctors are in-network, what the plan covers, and how much of the deductible has been met, so the disclosure could inform without truly empowering patients at the point of care.

Insurers and employers argued in broader price-transparency debates that publishing negotiated rates is trade-secret information and could raise prices, since providers seeing competitors' rates might push for higher payments — a cost that would eventually flow back to premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — letting patients see real prices before care — is real but modest: the bill covers disclosure only, with no mechanism making prices comparable, personalized, or available through an easy-to-use tool, and it exempts nothing but also fixes nothing else about medical billing. The cost falls on insurers and employers in compliance work, and possibly on premiums if rate disclosure changes provider negotiations. A reasonable idea, but narrow.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, sent to the Senate health committee, and nothing ever happened to it — no hearing, no vote, no floor action before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Braun introduced the True Price Act on March 27, 2019, to require insurers to disclose negotiated rates and cost-sharing to enrollees.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day.
It attracted no cosponsors, and the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer health plans are better off: they never had to publish their negotiated rates or lose the confidentiality of those rates. Patients who wanted price transparency before care got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, whose rates stayed confidential

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it read twice and referred to committee; no senator joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration after it was referred to his committee.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Industry affected by the disclosure mandate
against.what_they_did: Would have borne the cost of publishing negotiated rates; industry groups opposed public disclosure of negotiated rates in the broader price-transparency debate of this period.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by one Republican, drew no cosponsors from either party, and was never voted on, so no partisan pattern ever formed.

industries.note: Insurers would have to publish the negotiated rates they pay for every covered service and disclose cost-sharing to enrollees, ending the confidentiality of those rates. Patients currently face medical bills without ever seeing these numbers, which is why transparency rules like this are fought over.

Group health plans are covered by the same disclosure requirement, so large employers that self-insure would have had to publish their negotiated rates too. Some would see it as a compliance burden; others as a check on insurers and providers overcharging their plans.

The bill itself regulates insurers, but publishing insurer-negotiated rates exposes how widely provider prices vary and how far below list prices actual payments sit. Providers negotiating with insurers would gain a reference point — which tends to push payments up — while their steep list prices would look even less defensible.
